page.title: Day 11 against Neave's manual
page.standfirst_html: Every flag the comparator raised for Day 11, adjudicated against N.Day.11.18Jan20.pdf — the extracted text for wording, and sixteen page images for numbers, emphasis, and the two things pdftotext cannot read reliably: a decorative cover banner whose vector text extracts scrambled, and the clock-annotated contents page. The defects are mostly single wrong page numbers in Neave's own cross-references to The New Economics, DemDim and Bill Scherkenbach's book — seven of them — plus a handful of word substitutions, one of which ("mere" read as "more") comes close to reversing Deming's point. The other large group is emphasis: this day underlines far more than it italicises, and the site's existing restorations only caught about half of it. Decide each one; export the file; I make the edits and open the PR.

sections.title: Emphasis, found only in the page images
sections.note_html: Day 11 underlines far more than it italicises in Neave's asides, and pdftotext discards underlines exactly as it discards italics and bold — invisible to every automated flag in this epic.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: … the much wiser and more fruitful reaction would be to wonder: “Why is he saying this?”—… And then you’ll have really learned something new—and fruitful.
items.site_html: … both set in roman on the site.
items.proposal: ... the much wiser and more fruitful reaction would be to wonder: "*Why* is he saying this?"---... And then you'll have *really* learned something new---and fruitful.
items.evidence_html: Both italics carry real emphasis in Neave's own voice: *Why* stresses the word he wants the reader to lean on in that internal question, and *really* underlines that the learning is genuine, not superficial. Confirmed on the page image, printed p2.

items.evidence_html: Bold in the source, printed p5, contrasting with merely *having* information — the emphasis is on putting it to work. The neighbouring word “does” a few lines above is bold in the source the same way and is already marked up as `<em>` on the site, so `<em>` (matching that existing local convention) is proposed here too rather than `<strong>`.

items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image: PDF p3 is a clock-annotated itinerary listing every section with its own page number, duplicating text that also appears as the real heading later in the PDF. The comparator sometimes matches a PDF sentence against this listing rather than its real content-page counterpart, so the trailing “(p N)”, the time-range subtitle, and TOC-only phrasing (“Step 2: Dr Deming's May 1990 version” without its “Area 1,”/“Part D,” prefix) show up as “missing” or “altered” against QMD text that is, on its real page, complete and correctly worded. Same root cause behind all five missing-content gaps and both altered flags here.

items.chip: Decorative cover banner, scrambled by pdftotext
items.source_html: FIRST / SECOND / FIRST / PROJECT / PROJECT / continued (pdftotext's reading order of a stylised graphic)
items.site_html: ### SECOND PROJECT CONTINUED, with the matching banner image `second-project-continued-banner.png`
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image: this is a graphic design element, not linear prose. pdftotext extracts its embedded vector text in scrambled order (“SECOND FIRST PROJECT”), which is why it doesn't string-match the site's correctly-worded heading. Figure fidelity itself is #725's territory; this is only the caption text.

items.evidence_html: Checked against the page image: the alt-text/caption accurately describes the seven-word circular diagram (Theory, Question, Data, Prediction, Knowledge, Action, Wisdom) exactly as drawn. Legitimate site-only accessibility content describing a figure, not invented material.
